765.label: In each middlegame the player moves a piece off (or fails to take up) a critical defensive post—removing a king/key-square defender, blocking the king's own escape, or leaving a piece unguarded—letting the opponent crash through with either forced mate (boards 1,2,4,7,9) or decisive material loss (boards 3,5,6,8,10); the piece moved (rook 3, queen 2, knight 2, pawn/king/bishop) and the concrete outcome vary too much to name a single piece or result, but the core defensive-neglect mistake is consistent.

767.label: The player chooses a tempting forcing check instead of the objectively best move (usually a quiet, trading, or stronger capturing move), which typically backfires by hanging material or walking into mate and sometimes merely settles for a smaller advantage; the only reliable invariant is that the played move is always a check.

730.label: Fires on moves that ignore the opponent's best immediate response—a capture, forcing trade, or tactic (frequently a knight fork/recapture)—which in most cases drops the player's own material but in others merely throws away a winning advantage via an unfavorable trade or passive retreat; mixed in piece and outcome.

738.label: A piece/pawn is moved off the square where it was defending material, supporting a pawn, or attacking a key piece — but the result is inconsistent: ~5 boards hang own material (queen, bishop, rook) while the rest merely miss a faster win/draw or allow decisive passed pawns, so the feature is mixed.

780.label: In a roughly equal opening, the player captures a defended pawn (most often on d7/e7) with a minor piece—usually the bishop—and after the recapture has surrendered a full piece for a pawn; a minority of boards instead show a bishop trade or a knight capture that either loses material or throws away a win.

790.label: In a (usually losing) rook endgame, the player makes a move that fails to blockade or stop the opponent's passed pawn — typically misplacing the rook instead of getting it behind the pawn — allowing it to promote; a minority of boards instead permit a mate or hang a rook.

786.label: Mixed self-inflicted-loss feature: most often a queen or king move that vacates a key defensive square or walks the king into trouble, allowing checkmate or loss of material (boards 1,3,4,7,8,10), but it also fires on non-forcing tempo/prophylactic moves that miss a clean win (g5, g6, Kf1) and one positional rook concession (Rf7), so the core is fuzzy though the queen is the central piece in nearly every refutation.

708.label: Genuinely mixed: in an endgame the player chooses a tempting forcing move — a capture (1,2,4,6,8) or a flashy/spite check (3,5,9) — instead of the correct continuation, which hangs a piece in ~4 cases (Q/B/N, no single dominant piece), misses a forced mate or perpetual in ~4 cases, and ruins a winning plan with a quiet move in ~2 cases (Ra1, g4); position-state is also split (≈4 winning, 2 drawn, 4 already losing), so the SEE 'winning/hung/capture 100%' signature overstates a single direction.

784.label: Plays a forcing, tempting check (most often a knight fork/discovery, sometimes a rook or queen) that throws away a winning position — usually the checking piece is simply captured, occasionally the check merely substitutes for a stronger winning capture or trade.

793.label: A developing/pinning move (usually a bishop, often Bb4 or Bb5) that leaves own material undefended and losing, while ~3 of 10 instead skip a clear win or mate; the hung piece varies so no single piece is decisive.

774.chip: Queen check instead of winning capture

782.chip: Mixed: hangs material or squanders edge
782.label: Genuinely mixed opening/early-middlegame feature: ~4 boards hang own material to a recapture/fork/zwischenzug (varied piece: bishop, knight, queen), ~3 miss a clean win or pawn break (fxe5, c5, c6), and ~3 squander an edge via a bad trade or positional drift — no single piece or mistake type dominates, and the SEE 'bishop/capture/losing 100%' signature is contradicted by the actual moves.

792.label: The feature mostly fires at critical endgame moments where the player botches a passed pawn or promotion—losing a pawn race (board 2), entering a lost pawn ending by grabbing material (board 3), promoting into a knight that captures the queen (board 4), or playing a king move instead of the winning immediate promotion (boards 5-6)—but it also catches two unrelated missed Bxg7 winning-exchange tactics (boards 7-8) and one false positive where the played capture was actually best (board 1), so it does not resolve to a single clean mistake.

800.chip: Missed faster forcing win (often a check)

812.chip: Quiet pawn move skips decisive play
812.label: From a winning position the engine plays a slow prophylactic/luft pawn push (h3/g3/h4/g6) instead of the decisive move — usually a forcing capture or forced mate it fails to grab (6/10), but in the rest failing to save its own attacked piece (4/10) — with the piece involved varying.

810.label: A middlegame material error—most often failing to grab a free or winning capture (frequently an enemy knight or bishop), but in a sizable minority hanging its own piece or walking into a knight fork—with a knight involved in the decisive tactic on most boards; direction is genuinely mixed between missed wins and self-hangs.

825.label: The player makes a tempting capture or aggressive (usually knight) move that pulls a piece off a critical defensive duty — guarding the king's zone or shielding a hanging piece — and the refutation either forces mate (about half the boards) or wins the now-undefended material in the rest.

803.label: In a winning or drawing position the player plays a hasty forcing move—either a purposeless check (1,2,3) or a greedy / wrong-move-order capture (5,6,7,8,9,10)—that throws away the advantage, most often by hanging own material (frequently the queen) to a recapture or zwischenzug, with a couple of cases that simply miss a forced mate or stronger win.

826.label: In all 10 boards the queen is the decisive piece, but the player's error is mixed: ~5 hang material to a queen capture, ~3 miss capturing an exposed/hanging enemy queen, and ~2 are bad queen trades or failed attacks on the queen — unified by misjudging a queen interaction rather than one consistent direction.

830.label: The player makes a pawn move—almost always one attacking an enemy piece—instead of an available forcing line, missing a winning tactic or mate in most boards and hanging own material to the refutation in the rest.

819.label: In king-and-pawn / passed-pawn endgames the player most often marches the king the wrong direction — blockading incorrectly, too slowly, or stepping away from where it's needed — squandering a win or worsening a loss, while the rest are a mixed bag (releasing pawn tension, trading a knight/bishop for a passer, hanging a knight).

824.label: In already-lost positions the player — most often with a rook — makes a move that abandons a defensive duty and ignores the opponent's immediate decisive threat, usually allowing a forced checkmate (6/10) and otherwise dropping material (3/10), instead of the sole saving resource.

833.label: The feature mostly fires on premature pawn promotions (usually to a queen on an open file) that get immediately captured by a rook/king, throwing away a winning endgame when an intermediate check (zwischenzug) was needed first; a couple of boards instead show a hasty capture that trades away a forced mate, and one board isn't a blunder at all.

853.label: Fires on rook moves played to attack/challenge the opponent's queen, which backfire by abandoning a defensive duty (usually hanging the player's own material, occasionally missing a stronger tactic instead).

869.label: Fires on king moves in king-and-pawn endgames; about half are genuine blunders where the king goes to the wrong square (loses the opposition or fails to occupy the pawn's promotion/blockade square, letting the pawn queen), while the other half are 0cp non-blunders, so the feature is fuzzy and needs review.

865.label: In the opening the player botches a material/capture decision with a knight usually the focal piece — most often declining to grab a free hanging piece (6/10, e.g. skipping cxd5/dxe4/bxc3), but in ~4/10 instead hanging its own piece or ignoring a refuting tactic (Nc3 into dxc3, Nf6 into exf6, d6 into Qh5+); direction is genuinely mixed, flag for review.

844.label: In a winning opening the player plays a passive or careless non-best move that abandons the strongest continuation — usually a winning queen capture or mate (~6/10) — or else lets their own queen/piece fall in the refutation (~4/10), with a queen central to the decisive play on nearly every board.

863.label: In favorable positions the player chooses a simplifying capture or queen/piece trade that throws away the advantage—about six boards skip a stronger forcing tactic (fork/deflection/discovery) while four hang or walk into material loss, so the direction is genuinely mixed.

862.label: A material-grabbing capture or a careless king move neglects king safety and walks into a forced mate or decisive king attack, most often a back-rank or promotion-check mate.

889.label: A self-inflicted opening/early-middlegame move that loses the player's own material—most boards drop a piece outright (knight on e5/h6, queen on f2, bishop left undefended) or greedily grab a pawn and drop more (boards 1,2,3,5,7,10), with a couple also entombing a piece (8) or giving back material in a clumsy exchange (9), while two are really positional/missed-win errors (boards 4,6), so the hung piece type and exact mechanism vary.

907.label: From a winning/advantageous position the player plays a passive 'safe' move and misses the single forcing winning continuation—most often a passed-pawn breakthrough or promotion race in the endgame (e5+, g4, e2)—occasionally instead hanging own material or blundering into mate, converting a clear win into a loss.

885.label: In a mostly winning position, a quiet/greedy move (often king centralization or a pawn-grab) overlooks the position's tactic, usually hanging the player's own material or walking into mate (king ×3, knight ×3, queen ×1), though ~3/10 instead simply miss a winning capture — so direction is mixed.

876.label: In winning endgames the player fails to convert—hanging its own queen or missing a winning queen capture/mate—with a queen central to nearly every board's decisive tactics, though 3 of 10 are actually best moves (not mistakes) and the direction (hang vs. miss) is split.

880.chip: Slow rook maneuver over forcing move
880.label: The player prefers a slow, thematic rook maneuver (doubling on an open file, a rook lift, or a rook swing) over the concrete forcing continuation—most often missing a forced mate or decisive win (6/10), but in about a third of cases the slow rook move itself hangs a piece (knight, pawn+tempo, or even the queen), so the outcome direction is mixed even though the misbehavior is consistent.

893.label: From a favorable position the player chooses a safe but inferior continuation—frequently a needless/wrong queen trade or a missed stronger check or fork—squandering the win rather than hanging material outright (one board is an outright greedy capture).

910.label: Fires on a queen check (occasionally a non-checking queen move) in an endgame that backfires—most often it allows/offers a queen trade into a lost pawn endgame (1,5,6,7,9), but it also covers checks that waste a tempo and help the enemy king instead of grabbing a free pawn or winning resource (2,3,10) and ones that outright hang the queen (4,8); the only constant is the player's queen in decisive endgame play, so the specific error is genuinely mixed.

890.label: In a (usually winning) position the player fires off a tempting forcing move—most often a queen check—instead of the precise continuation, throwing the advantage away by either missing a forced mate/win (boards 1,2,4,5,10) or hanging the queen/rook (boards 3,6,7,9), so the unifying element is the impulsive check/forcing move rather than any single piece or outcome.

905.label: Mixed feature that mostly fires on throwing away a better/winning position by hanging own material — knight (boards 2,3,4), bishop (7,9), or pawn (8) — but ~4/10 are instead tempo-loss or greedy captures (1,5,6,10) that miss the decisive move rather than directly hanging a piece, so no single piece or position-state dominates.

914.chip: Poor rook move loses holdable position (rook)
914.label: The player mishandles their rook—usually by placing it passively (1,2,9,10), occasionally by hanging it (6,8) or trading it into a lost pawn endgame (3,5,7)—surrendering the rook's activity and converting a drawn or defensible position (often an endgame) into a loss; the rook is the decisive piece in nearly every board even though the precise mechanism is mixed.

945.label: In a 100%-winning position the player plays a safe/natural pawn push or king move that throws away an available forced checkmate (mate-in-1 or mate-in-2), though the feature is mixed: ~7/10 are missed forced mates, 1 loses a win via wrong move order, and 2 are instead self-inflicted material hangs (e7 dropping the queen, Rc1 allowing Bxb4+).

909.label: Player makes a capture (or pawn move) that opens a file/diagonal toward their own king or strips a key defender, exposing material or the king to a decisive tactic — though several boards are already-lost positions where the move is near-best, plus one pure positional error, making the core only partially uniform.

939.label: On most boards the player overlooks a tactical refutation (recapture, fork, or opened diagonal) and loses their own material — but the hung piece varies (bishop, knight, queen) and 3-4 boards are instead missed wins or bad trades/endgames rather than clean hangs, so a human should review.

932.chip: Missed fastest win in won endgame (king move)
932.label: In a winning endgame the player makes a slow king (or other) move that keeps the win but squanders the fastest forced route — typically a pawn promotion or forced mate — though several flagged boards are negligible/non-blunders and one is a flat hung rook.

963.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a slow king move instead of the decisive ...f5/e5 pawn break, missing the win or only draw — but ~half the boards are non-blunders where the king move is actually optimal (plus one unrelated rook-trade error).

922.label: Fires on aggressive, active-looking moves (often pawn thrusts like ...e5/...f5/...g4, but also rook sorties and a greedy ...Qxd4+) that collapse an equal or winning position; most are punished by the player's own material being captured in the refutation (queen on d4, rook on d6/g7, bishop on g2), while a few are pure positional weakenings (e5/f5 ceding key squares) or missed wins (Kc7/g4+ skipping a material-winning capture), so the mechanism is mixed and no single piece or state is consistent.

942.label: A bishop is developed to harass the enemy queen with apparent tempo in the opening, but the move is unsound: in about 60% of cases it hangs material (an undefended b7/b2/g7 pawn, or the bishop itself via an Nxf6+ deflection), and in the rest it merely wastes tempo letting the queen improve or skips a stronger move.

929.label: In opening positions built around a Bg4-pin on Nf3 (where Bxf3 — or keeping f3 pressure — was the right resolving move, ~7/10 boards), the player makes a move ignoring the tension that either drops a minor piece in the multi-move refutation (~6/10, e.g. Nxd4 then Bxg4) or fatally exposes the uncastled king/structure (~4/10); the f3-knight/Bg4 pin is the recurring element, but the resulting mistake type is mixed and 3 boards (trapped Ba5, hanging Be4, Nd5) don't fit the pin theme at all.

911.label: A forcing/aggressive move (most often a bishop capture, occasionally a check or pawn break) made from a winning or favorable position that squanders the advantage — roughly 6/10 boards by leaving the player's own piece hanging (frequently the queen) and ~4/10 by missing a stronger capture or a forced mate, so direction is genuinely mixed.

894.label: In a mostly winning/holdable endgame the player makes a king step or queen move that loses material on the 2nd-3rd move of the refutation—usually the queen, via a knight fork or by leaving it undefended—but the feature is mixed: ~6/10 hang material, 2 are missed forced mates, one is a tempo slip, and one is a false positive.

980.label: Plays a quiet/non-forcing move (pawn push, piece reposition, or natural capture) instead of the available forcing tactical break, squandering a winning or favorable position; the piece moved varies, and in ~3 of 10 losing/tense cases the same passivity or careless capture instead allows mate or hangs a rook.

970.label: Player plays a slow, greedy, or natural move that overlooks a decisive forcing resource — most often a checkmate (5 mate-in-1, 2 allowed mates) — with the remaining boards missing a winning or drawing resource in passed-pawn endgames.

981.label: The feature mainly fires on moves that leave a piece undefended and lose it — frequently a bishop, often by walking a defender (queen/rook) off its guarding duty — but it is mixed, also firing on ~3 pure tempo/positional squanders and one ignored back-rank/diagonal mate threat.

1021.label: In critical 'only-move' positions (nearly every board notes a single good move within 50cp) the player picks a plausible but inferior move instead of the unique precise — usually forcing/material-winning — continuation; direction is mostly 'missed the best move' across winning, drawn and losing starts, but a few cases (Nxh5+ twice, Rb5) also actively hang material in the multi-move refutation, so it's somewhat mixed.

1032.label: Fires on king moves in already-losing endgames (mostly rook endings); about half are non-mistakes or sub-10cp inaccuracies that are often the engine's top move, while the rest are catastrophic king moves that walk into forced mates or lose material via varied mechanisms (skewer, missed free-queen capture), so the only reliable constant is 'king move in a losing endgame', not any single mistake.

1056.label: A natural-looking repositioning move (often a queen relocation) that overlooks the position's decisive tactic—either skipping a winning shot (boards 1,3,4,7,9) or deserting a key attacker/defender and hanging material in the refutation (boards 2,5,8,10)—so it fires roughly evenly on both 'missed win' and 'hung own' and is genuinely mixed in direction.

1069.label: In an endgame the player advances a pawn that is immediately captured, converting a drawn or winning position into a loss, though several boards instead fire on king moves that hang another piece or on non-decisive captures.

1073.label: The player makes a quiet, passive, or retreating move — frequently pulling a queen, knight, or bishop off a dominant square — and overlooks the decisive forcing tactic that would win material or deliver mate.

966.label: In a winning/better middlegame the player throws the advantage away — most often by greedily capturing or 'eliminating a dangerous' pawn (7/10) — but the punishment is mixed: about half the boards simply miss a decisive material-winning capture (Nxe7, Kxc5, Bxd5, Nxe3) while the rest hang own material straight into a mating net (Rxf2, Qxb6, g4, Qxf3), so direction (missed-win vs self-hang) is not consistent.

1059.label: In a winning/equal opening the player makes an overreaching developing or attacking move that loses material — usually hanging a minor piece (bishop or knight) to a one-move capture, though several cases are pawn/tempo lunges or an unsound sac that drop the advantage instead.

1076.label: The player makes a tempting capture—most often grabbing the opponent's queen—that backfires, either hanging material to a recapture, knight fork, or back-rank mate (7/10), or trading away a clearly winning advantage (3/10).

1106.chip: Missed simplifying rook liquidation, won endgame (rook)
1106.label: In winning endgames the player declines the simplifying rook capture/sacrifice (usually taking Black's last minor piece, most often a knight) that liquidates into a trivially won pawn endgame, instead making a natural king or pawn move.

982.label: The player repeatedly converts a winning/equal position into an equal-or-losing one by giving up a piece — most often an active knight (7/10) — either trading off their strongest piece or skipping a stronger tactic (boards 1,2,3,4,7,10) or hanging a piece outright (boards 5,6,8,9), so the mechanism is genuinely mixed between trade/missed-win and self-inflicted hang.

1110.label: In a winning position the player plays a quiet safe move and skips a winning capture (frequently a king grabbing a hanging bishop), but the feature is mixed — about 6/10 are missed winning captures while 4/10 are unrelated tempo/positional/endgame drops.

1075.label: In mostly-winning middlegames the player botches the decisive moment with the queen at the center of the action — about half the boards miss a forced mate/material win by playing a quiet king or queen move, the rest actively hang or trade away the queen (or grab material into mate); direction is genuinely mixed, so review.

1143.label: The feature mostly fires on an over-ambitious pawn advance (87% pawn moves) that either hangs own material or causes a large eval collapse, but the lost unit varies (queen on 1, exchange/rook on 6-7, pawn on 9) and it misfires on a bishop move (2) and one fully-correct push (10), so no single piece can be named.

1120.chip: Missed decisive move when winning (often free capture)
1120.label: In winning positions (mostly endgames) the player skips the decisive move—most often failing to capture an undefended enemy piece (queen/rook/bishop/knight, varies), but a sizable minority are tempo-wasting rook checks plus one outright self-hang and one non-blunder, so the feature is mixed and only loosely centered on missed wins.

1113.label: From a winning or better position, the player plays a tempting active move (capture/fork/check/knight sortie, a knight in 7/10) that squanders the edge—either hanging the piece outright (~4/10) or trading off the key piece into equality/loss (~6/10); mixed between hangs and trades, hence review.

1144.label: On about half the boards the player greedily grabs material—usually the enemy queen—and overlooks a forced refutation (mate-in-one/few or a missed perpetual/win), but the rest are a mixed bag of hanging a piece via a non-capturing king/bishop move, a failed sacrifice, and pointless 'hope' checks, so the feature is not cleanly one mistake.

1134.label: In a winning-or-better position the player makes a move that exposes its own king or strips a key defender, allowing a decisive check or forced mate (boards 2,3,4,5,9,10); but the set is mixed, with outliers throwing a win into an insufficient-material draw (1), hanging a bishop (6), trading into a lost K+P endgame (7), and a quiet positional/tempo loss (8), so no single hung/missed piece is the invariant.

1131.label: In sharp, usually-winning positions the player throws away the result, roughly half the time by hanging its own material (frequently the queen) and half by missing a forced win or free capture, with no consistent direction.

1171.label: In mostly level (drawn) middlegames/endings the player picks a natural, passive developing or file-occupying move and overlooks a forcing capture or rook/minor-piece exchange that would win material or equalize (boards 1-7,9), with two cases instead grabbing a capture that walks into a refutation (8,10); the decisive piece varies, so the core is a missed forcing capture/exchange rather than one piece or direction.

1168.label: The player makes a capture meant to rip open the enemy king's pawn shield (most often a bishop or pawn taking on g6), but the move is unsound and loses their own material—usually squandering a winning position—though a couple of boards instead miss a winning tactic.

1173.label: The player makes a move—most often retreating or deflecting the queen (6/10 are queen moves), or pushing a pawn that vacates/opens a line (b3, c3, a5)—that strips their own king of its last defender or shelter, allowing decisive checks or mate; 2-3 boards instead miss a forcing win (Qe5+, Ne6+, Qxe5).

1146.label: Fires on queen-driven tactics centered on one undefended piece (usually a bishop, the queen decisive on nearly every board), but direction is mixed: ~6/10 miss a free queen capture of an enemy piece while ~4/10 hang the player's own piece.

1179.chip: Ignores threat; hangs piece or allows mate
1179.label: In an already losing or critical position, the player plays a non-defensive 'active' move (pawn push, centralization, king relocation) that ignores the decisive threat, and is punished either by losing a hanging piece (most often a rook — boards 3,8,10 and the undefended rooks in 5,9) or by walking into a forced mate (often back-rank — boards 4,5,7,9,6); the two failure modes are genuinely mixed but share the same root of not addressing the critical threat.

1170.chip: Squanders winning position via material decision
1170.label: From a winning or advantageous position the player makes a poor material decision—most often an unfavorable trade (frequently the queen) but also failed/under-promotions and a hung knight on a defended pawn—collapsing the advantage; the mechanism is mixed with no single piece or move-type as the clear invariant.

1154.label: In already-difficult endgames the player makes a self-inflicting pawn advance or piece relocation that abandons a strong/defensive square, worsening the position or losing material over the next moves, though the specific piece and error subtype (material hang, tempo loss, or back-rank mate) vary too much to name one confidently.

1182.label: Mixed feature: a knight is the decisive piece in nearly every board, but the precise error varies — roughly half the positions hang/lose the player's own knight (immediately as in Nd3/Nc3, or over 2-3 moves of the refutation via move-order slips like Rd3/Rg1 dropping the d6 outpost), while the other half fail to capture or trade a key enemy knight (missed Bxg5, Bxc3, Nxe4), in each case throwing away a winning or equal position.

1183.label: In an endgame the defending side plays an inferior move that fails the best defensive resource (a saving capture, drawing trade, or king centralization), converting a draw to a loss or accelerating a forced mate — though several boards are already lost and a couple are not real errors.

1205.label: In an endgame the player makes a losing move—usually hanging a piece (most often the rook) or wasting a tempo/defender in a passed-pawn promotion race—turning a difficult-or-drawn position into a clear loss.

1147.chip: Quiet non-capturing move, misses only save
1147.label: In drawn-or-losing positions the player makes a passive non-capturing king/pawn/rook move (often declining a saving capture) that misses the single precise save, with the punishment varying across boards—hanging a queen/rook, walking into back-rank/king-trap mate, or losing a drawn pawn endgame—so it's a mixed 'losing-move' feature (board 5 is a false positive where the played move was best).

1196.chip: Passive opening move ignores urgent demand
1196.label: In the opening, plays a natural quiet developing or repositioning move that ignores the position's urgent demand (an unresolved threat, a pin, central tension, or a winning tactic), either hanging material or squandering a win — but the piece moved and whether material is hung vs. a win is missed both vary across boards, so no single piece or direction can be named.

1169.label: The player makes a move that fails to address the opponent's existing decisive threat—most often an immediate king-side mating attack (Qg2#, back-rank Rd1#, etc.), sometimes a material-winning tactic—either by playing an unrelated move, removing a critical defender, or stepping the king/queen into the attack, and is crushed; the punished outcome varies between mate (~6/10) and material loss (~4/10), so no single piece is decisive on every board.

1197.label: Player grabs material (usually a capture) or follows an own plan instead of the strongest continuation—most often a forced mate or decisive, frequently queen-led attack—squandering a winning position, with a couple of boards instead being tempo/fork blunders that simply hang material.

1223.label: Fires on early opening queen sorties (Qb3/Qb6/Qf3); in ~75% the exposed queen is punished by a knight fork or Bxf7+ break that loses material, while ~25% are winning positions where the slow queen move skips an immediate Bxf7+/Nxe5 tactic — so the piece (queen) is constant but the direction is mixed.

1195.label: A critical-position move that throws away a winning or drawn game, most often by hanging the player's own material (7/10), with a bishop in the decisive line on 7/10 boards (either hung or as the missed saving move), the remaining boards instead missing a forced win.

1211.label: Fires on slow/quiet/greedy moves played instead of an available forcing continuation (often a check, but also a capture or promotion), squandering a winning or advantageous position; the moved piece and exact mechanism vary, and at least one board is actually the correct move.

1226.label: A developing or pawn move in the opening that fatally exposes the player's king/queen line — in 7/10 boards it opens the light-square diagonal allowing a devastating Qh5+/Qh4#, while in 3/10 it leaves the queen on c3 with the king on e1 to be won by a ...Bb4 pin; the mechanism is mixed, but the queen (as attacker or as the pinned victim) is the decisive piece on nearly every board.

1234.chip: Wrong-way king move, lost pawn endgame
1234.label: In already-losing king-and-pawn endgames (mover is losing on all 10 boards), the player makes a king move in the wrong direction — passive/retreating or toward the wrong wing — losing the king-activity/counter-race instead of running the best defensive march; it's fuzzy because 3 of the 10 boards (2, 5, 6) lose ~0–15cp and the named move is essentially best, so the feature mostly fires on 'misdirected king in lost pawn endgames' rather than a clean blunder.

1215.label: In positions revolving around a queen that is en prise (75% winning), the player mishandles it — either failing to capture the opponent's free queen (boards 2,4,5,6,9) or removing a defender that leaves its own queen hanging (boards 1,3,8), with two queen-check/no-trade king-safety variants (7,10); the queen is the decisive piece on nearly every board but the direction (missed-capture vs self-hang) is genuinely mixed.

1221.chip: Throws away advantage; often hangs bishop
1221.label: Genuinely mixed 'blunder' feature: about half the moves directly hang the player's own material (bishop ×3, queen ×2) to a 1-3 move tactic, while the other half are positional or king-safety errors (allowing Ndb5/Ba3, premature breaks, Bf7+ on an uncastled king) that squander a winning or equal position; a bishop appears in the decisive line of most boards but in varying roles, so no single hung piece can anchor the label.

1233.label: Across these middlegame boards the player makes a tempting active move—usually a check, capture, or trade-offer (rook/bishop/knight/queen all appear)—that throws away a winning or equal position, sometimes hanging material outright (boards 4, 9, 10) but more often trading off the key attacking piece or missing a stronger tactic / the only saving move; piece and exact mechanism vary, so it's genuinely mixed rather than a single-piece hang.

1207.label: Mixed 'blunders the win' feature in sharp middlegames: 5 boards hang material outright (Rf4, g3, Qe6+, Qxe2, Bb4) and 5 skip a winning capture (Rxa3+, Qxd8+ x2, Bxf8, dxe5); the only consistent element is that the queen sits in the decisive line on ~9/10 boards, but its role varies too much to fix a single direction.

1241.label: The player relocates a piece—most often a knight (~7/10)—to a square where it is captured outright or refuted by a short follow-up tactic, losing material; a few boards are positional/tempo self-inflicted losses rather than clean hangs.

1232.label: A self-inflicted blunder, usually an over-ambitious forcing move (frequently a check or knight sortie) that hangs the player's own material—the specific piece varies (knight, queen, exchange)—while a couple of boards instead miss a defense or a forced win.

1228.chip: Skips forcing line at critical moment
1228.label: At sharp tactical positions the player rejects the forcing best move (usually a check or capture) for a slow, natural, or greedy alternative, either squandering a winning tactic (boards 1,3,4,6,8) or walking into a forced material loss/mate (boards 2,5,7,9,10).

1261.label: Most boards play a move that leaves one of the player's own pieces undefended and lost — immediately or within the refutation (the d5-knight, the g4/g6 bishop, or the a5-knight) — but the hung piece varies and three boards are instead a missed-win capture, a tempo slip, or a bad positional trade, so it's best named generically as 'hangs a piece.'

1240.label: In already-winning positions the player plays a premature forcing check or non-capturing move instead of first making the clean capture/trade, throwing away tempo or hanging a piece — most often the bishop — though boards 2, 3 and 9 are not actually blunders, so the pattern is partly noise.

1242.label: In a critical (mostly winning) position the player overlooks the single decisive move — a free capture (Nxh4/Qxg5), a saving castle (O-O), a king escape, a forcing check, or the right capture/move-order — and plays a passive or wrong move that squanders the win or walks into mate; ~8/10 are pure omissions, but 2 boards (Qe8, f3) are self-inflicted hangs, so direction is mixed.

1280.label: In winning endgames with pawn tension, the player captures (or plays a slow waiting move) to release the tension instead of the winning pawn advance/lock or break (f5/g6/g5/a5/hxg6), throwing away a forced mate or win — but the feature also fires on several boards where the capture is a 0cp non-blunder, so it really detects 'released pawn tension in a won position' regardless of whether it actually costs the win.

1267.label: From an equal middlegame, the player makes a move (often skipping the neutralizing ...Bxe5/...Bxe4) that lets a knight fork or infiltrate — or leaves their own knight hanging — dropping material within two or three moves.

1263.label: From a winning (75%) or drawn (25%) position the player throws away the advantage — via a slow/king or rook move that misses the decisive shot, a greedy capture, or a bad trade — with the queen central to the decisive line/refutation in most boards, though the exact mechanism (missed win vs. hung piece vs. losing trade) is mixed.

1283.label: Fires on moves that throw away a favorable/winning position by not finding the best continuation, but the mechanism is mixed: most often missing a stronger tactical or tempo-gaining move (6/10), sometimes outright hanging a piece (2/10), and sometimes trading off a key restraining bishop into an enemy passed pawn (2/10).

1278.chip: Quiet move skips saving queen trade
1278.label: A passive, non-forcing repositioning move (usually the queen, sometimes the king) that ignores a forcing resource—most often a game-saving queen trade/simplification (Qxg3, Qxf4, Qxe6), but in several boards a hanging knight or a winning exchange-sac—and is punished by losing material or squandering the advantage.

1303.label: In the opening Black plays a developing or pawn move (Nf6/Ng4/Ne4/f5/c6/Bd7/Qf6) that abandons or fails to advance the central e5 pawn instead of the freeing ...e4, and e5 falls (boards 1-7,9); boards 8 and 10 are instead White Bd3 tempo-loss moves that skip a central pawn break (d5/cxd5), so the e5-hang core is ~8/10.

1306.label: The feature most often fires when the player makes a slow/passive move that fails to capture a trapped enemy knight (5/10: g7, g2, b3, b3, b7), squandering a winning advantage; a knight is in the decisive play of nearly every board, but the direction is mixed—3 boards instead hang the player's own piece via a counting/move-order error (Nd4, Rxa6 bishop, b4-Qf6 rook) and 2 are pure positional give-backs (e4, d6).

1298.label: Genuinely mixed feature firing on over-optimistic, aggressive moves that backfire—most cleanly knights chasing a queen or going to the rim and losing tempo (1,2,3,6,7), but it also includes defender-removal/hangs (4,10), a back-rank lapse (5), and unsound sacrifices (8,9); knight is the moved or key piece in ~6/10, and material loss usually comes 2-3 moves deep in the refutation rather than immediately.

1299.label: An imprecise move—most often a kingside g/h pawn push or capture—that loses tempo or wrecks the player's own pawn structure and squanders a winning or near-equal position rather than cleanly hanging material, though about 2/10 boards instead drop a pawn/piece to a tactic (knight fork, undefended pawn).

1288.label: In drawn/winning endgames the player makes a non-self-hanging but inferior move that squanders the result—in the cleanest cases failing to capture a hanging piece (twice a free queen, once a bishop)—but several boards are positional or king-safety collapses (lost blockader, abandoned back rank, even a greedy capture into mate) rather than missed captures, so the feature is mixed.

1313.label: From a winning or strong middlegame position the player throws away the advantage, splitting roughly 60/40 between hanging a piece (frequently by moving a key defender) and missing a forced mate or win — the mechanism and piece are too mixed to name specifically.

1315.label: In an already-winning opening, the player throws away the advantage with a knight featuring in the decisive line of nearly every board, but direction is genuinely split—~6/10 are self-inflicted greedy/careless moves that lose the player's own material (sometimes over 2-3 moves) and ~4/10 are missed winning captures, with the relevant piece varying.

1275.chip: Squanders won position, missed forcing line
1275.label: From a winning position (mostly passed-pawn endgames) the player skips the one decisive forcing continuation—typically a promotion or rook trade/sac—and instead plays a passive or greedy move that lets the opponent escape (often by perpetual check), though the boards are mixed in how the win is thrown away.

1338.label: In a (mostly winning) endgame the player makes a quiet, non-forcing king/rook move (0% captures, 0% checks played) instead of the decisive continuation—a winning capture, a check, or the faster mate—squandering efficiency or material, though the set is mixed (two are 0cp false-positives, and a couple actually hang material rather than just being slow).

1343.chip: Lost endgame: passive move loses material/mate
1343.label: In an already-losing endgame, the player makes a passive or inferior move—most often a king move (7/10)—that abandons their own material (usually a pawn, sometimes a rook) or walks into a mating net, deepening the loss.

1361.label: A slow, tempo-wasting move—usually a non-urgent pawn push—fails to contest open files or force a rook trade, letting the opponent double rooks on the 7th/2nd rank (or otherwise activate decisively) and seize a winning initiative; two boards instead fire on a back-rank mate and a direct piece hang.

1355.label: From a (mostly winning) position the player never makes the available clean capture — they captured in 0/10 boards while the best move was a capture in 8/10 — instead playing a flashy check or a quiet king/rook reposition, which roughly half the time also hangs their own material; the declined-capture behavior is the consistent core, but the outcome (hangs vs. merely squanders) and piece involved both vary.

1332.label: In critical, mostly-losing endgames the feature fires when the player fails to play the single best move—either skipping a free material grab (queen captures Bxc3/Rxb8/Rxh4, the only-saving Kc4) or instead playing a move that hangs own material (rook on 4 & 8) or drifts into a lost positional/trade situation (5, 7, 10)—so the shared core is 'doesn't find the only good move and collapses,' but direction (missed-win vs self-hang vs slow loss) and piece both vary, warranting review.

1340.label: In drawn endgames the player makes a materially-safe move that overlooks the single best move — most often a free capture of a hanging enemy piece (usually the queen), occasionally the only drawing resource — turning equality into a loss.

1342.label: This is a mixed feature: 7/10 boards lose the player's own material on the refutation (most often a bishop left en prise or trapped, plus one exchange and one pawn) while 3/10 are 'safe' moves that simply skip a winning tactic — but a bishop is the decisive piece in the play on nearly every board (hung, trapped, or the key attacker/target).

1357.label: Genuinely mixed tactical-oversight feature: in ~6/10 boards (1,2,4,5,6,8) the player hangs their own material (queen, bishop, or knight) to a fork/deflection/overload, while in ~3/10 (3,7,10) it instead fires on missing a winning capture and one (9) is a move-order error—the common thread is mishandling a single critical piece whose capture/neutralization was the decisive move, but the direction (hang vs missed-win) and the piece both vary, so no single piece or state dominates.

1377.chip: Mistimed endgame king move (king, pawn race)
1377.label: Endgame king (or supporting pawn) moves in passed-pawn/promotion races where tempo and opposition are mishandled—often allowing a tempo-gaining check or a wrong promotion order—though several flagged positions are actually engine-approved non-blunders, so the feature is noisy.

1379.label: In the endgame the player plays a suboptimal move—most often a king move (6/10)—that fails to find the single best resource, splitting roughly between missed wins (missed forks/captures/mates or imprecise pawn breaks, ~7 boards) and self-inflicted losses (blowing a draw or hanging a piece, ~3 boards), so it's a general endgame-blunder feature rather than one specific mistake.

1351.label: Fires when a clearly stronger continuation exists (SAE floor: a material-winning move) but the player plays an inferior one instead — about half are passive or self-obstructing moves that simply miss the win, the rest hang own material or walk into a tactic; mechanism and piece vary, position usually unclear rather than already winning.

1345.label: Across its top boards the player passes up the engine's decisive capture (best move is a capture in 9/10), most often substituting a pointless check or a routine/wrong capture; direction is mixed — roughly 6 squander a clean win while 4 leave the player's own queen or rook to be taken, so this needs review.

1397.label: In difficult or already-losing middlegames, the player makes an over-ambitious or careless move (often a rook or knight move, sometimes castling) that either drops material to a tactic or removes the king's shield/escape, allowing decisive infiltration and accelerating the loss.

1381.chip: Trades off defensive rook in endgame
1381.label: In an endgame the player captures with the rook (usually a pawn, often with check), trading off or deflecting its own rook — the sole blockading/defensive resource — and converts a holdable or drawn position into a lost one; a minority of boards are non-trade endgame slips (a tempo-wasting check, a pawn move, or allowing an unfavorable queen trade).

1386.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player makes a king move or mistimed pawn capture that loses the passed-pawn race (tempo loss, king misplacement, or premature trade), but the feature is fuzzy — ~3/10 top boards are 0–13cp non-blunders in already-lost positions, two are pawn moves rather than king moves, and no piece is ever actually hung.

1366.label: Genuinely mixed feature: in mostly winning/better positions (winning 56%) the player chooses a natural-looking developing, repositioning or pawn-advancing move that throws away the advantage, but the mechanism splits roughly evenly — ~3 boards hang the player's own material with no consistent piece (pawn b2/h7, bishop g5, exchange via g6), ~3 boards skip a winning capture (Nxe4 #5, Qxd2 #6, Bxb7 #10), and ~4 boards lose tempo or allow an equalizing/tactical resource (#1,#4,#7,#8), so neither a single piece nor a single hang/miss mechanism dominates beyond 'plausible move forfeits the win.'

1383.label: Fires on king-and-pawn / promotion endgames where the king is the decisive piece on every board; the player's king move is often imprecise—throwing away the draw on some, the win on others—but roughly 3 of 10 are 0cp non-blunders and direction is mixed, so this is a fuzzy king-endgame feature rather than a clean blunder detector.

1403.label: In middlegame positions where a knight is the decisive tactical piece, the player loses the material balance two different ways: ~6/10 by hanging one of its own pieces (a knight in boards 1/3/8/10, a bishop in 6, a rook in 7 via Ne1+/Qxc2+) and ~4/10 by passing up a winning knight fork (the repeated 34-37.Nd6+ in boards 2/4/5/9, plus missed Nc3/Ne3 forks elsewhere); the direction is genuinely mixed (self-hang vs missed win, near 50/50 per the safe-46%/hangs-45% split), so the only firm common thread is that a knight sits at the center of the tactic on nearly every board.

1412.label: In endgames (mostly pawn endgames) the player squanders a decisive advantage—often a forced win or mate—by playing a hasty pawn advance instead of the precise converting move (frequently a king move, sometimes a better pawn break/capture or rook move), though a couple of boards involve non-pawn moves or already-lost positions.

1399.label: In winning opening positions the player squanders the advantage—most often by a premature trade (Bxe6/Bxc6) or quiet developing move that skips a decisive d-pawn advance/capture (d5/dxe7/dxc6)—but ~3 boards instead simply hang the player's own knight/bishop, so the mechanism is mixed (mostly missed-win, partly self-hang).

1459.label: Feature fires on king moves in king-and-pawn endgames where opposition/key-square control is decisive, but it's mixed: only ~4 of 10 (boards 1, 2, 3, 10) are genuine opposition-/key-square-losing blunders that turn a draw into a loss, while the other 6 are already-lost positions where the king move is a negligible (0–12cp) non-error that merely happens to occur in opposition-themed endgames.

1405.label: The player keeps choosing a quiet/repositioning move (very often a knight retreat or reroute) instead of the available forcing/active resource — a capture, check, fork, or pawn break — squandering a winning or holdable position, though a couple of boards instead hang material or grab a bad capture, so the mechanism is mixed.

1415.label: From winning positions the player usually makes a queen move that leaves the queen en prise to a direct or short-tactic capture (Bxd5, Nxg4, Bxg3, fork), though two boards are actually missed wins and one is a tempo/positional error rather than an outright hang.

1416.label: Genuinely mixed: in a decided position the player plays a quiet/non-forcing move that ignores the one critical resource — skipping a free capture of an undefended enemy rook (Rxh8/Qxd1/Rxh1/Qxc8/Qxe8, 6/10) or walking the king straight into a forced mate (Kh3/Kh2/exf4/Bh6, 4/10); no single piece or direction dominates, so review.

1426.label: Player skips the forcing Qa4+/Qa5+ diagonal check that exploits the loose enemy knight on b4 and the uncastled king, throwing away a winning advantage in 8/10 boards; the other 2 are the defensive flip side where the same b4-knight fork (Bc2/Bd3+/Nc2) wins material, so direction is mostly missed-win with a minor hung-material tail.

1431.label: On most boards the player grabs immediate material with a tempting capture (or premature pawn push), overlooking a more precise resource — an in-between check, a stronger capture, structural preservation, or even a forced mate — though a couple of boards instead fire on a passive/hanging move and one (Nxc5) isn't actually a mistake, so the feature is greedy-capture-leaning but mixed.

1484.label: Feature fires on forcing checks in already-winning endgames (7/10 are checks, position winning 100%); the intended 'mistake' is a tempo-losing check that spoils a faster mate/mating net, but it's genuinely mixed—5 of the checks are 0cp non-mistakes, and 3 boards aren't checks at all (Kh5 blunders a draw, b5 a minor pawn push, Qf2 a missed queen capture).

1501.label: In endgames (100% endgame, king moves 67%) the player makes a passive or retreating king move—occasionally a passive/over-eager rook move—that concedes tempo and activity instead of the active centralizing/restricting continuation; no material is hung (100% safe), with severity ranging from trivial 0–11cp slips to walking into a forced mate.

1494.label: A material error where a queen is decisive in nearly every position — most often hanging own material (frequently the queen) via a natural-looking move, but sometimes overlooking a free capture of the enemy queen.

1419.label: From a clearly winning position the player makes a non-forcing king or pawn move that throws away the win; this fires roughly half on direct material hangs (queen/rook/bishop/pawn vary — boards 1,3,7,10) and half on missed forcing conversions like intermezzo checks or correct move order (boards 2,4,5,6,8), with one board (9) not actually a mistake — so the unifying signal is 'squandered winning position,' not a specific hung piece.

1507.label: Player chooses a slow, non-forcing/preparatory move instead of the demanded concrete forcing continuation; in ~6/10 this squanders a winning tactic with own material staying safe, but in ~4/10 the quiet move actually allows the opponent to win material (hanging a piece or walking into a fork), and the piece/tactic involved varies board to board with no single recurring piece.

1457.chip: Greedy pawn grab blows won endgame (king)
1457.label: In a (mostly) winning endgame the player squanders the win by grabbing a pawn—usually with the king (6/10), which exposes a second pawn or abandons a defensive duty and is refuted by an immediate recapture—or by pushing a passer prematurely (3/10); mechanism is mixed, with one opening bishop-hang outlier.

1460.label: A move—frequently a queen move—that abandons a defensive duty or ignores a standing threat, hanging a piece or allowing mate in the refutation; the queen recurs in the decisive play of nearly every board even though the dropped unit varies, with two boards instead missing free material.

1489.label: Mixed self-defeating-blunder feature: fires when the player throws away a fine/winning position—most often by hanging or trapping own material or walking into a tactical/mating refutation (~67%), but also by missing a free winning capture (Qxe5, Kxf6) or making a losing forcing trade; the piece and exact motif vary board-to-board, with a mild lean toward greedy/forcing moves backfiring.

1443.label: The feature fires on a natural-looking rook move (7/10 are rook moves, 4 of them the same Ra8–d8 'activate on the open d-file' idea) that squanders a winning or equal position, but the punishing mechanism is genuinely mixed: ~4 boards hang own material in the refutation (knight on b5, h7 pawn, the exchange to Bxd8, c5 pawn via Nxc5+), ~2 simply miss a winning capture (Qxc7, Nxg5), and ~4 are bad trades/positional drifts (queen trade into a lost rook ending, abandoning the e-file to a passer, allowing Red7, or a near-zero inaccuracy), so neither a single hung piece nor a single direction dominates.

1512.chip: Passive king move misses forcing win
1512.label: In a won endgame the player makes a quiet/passive move (usually a king move) that skips a decisive forcing win — most often an immediate promotion-with-check or a forcing check/mate sequence — though several boards (notably 6 and 8, and the minor 2/7) are not actually blunders.

1503.label: In the opening the player mishandles a knight-centered tactic with a knight in the decisive line of every board — most often failing to apply the h3/h6 antidote to an enemy g5/g4 knight eyeing f7, but also walking into knight forks (Nc7+) or greedy/failed knight grabs — usually throwing away a winning advantage (and on a couple of boards missing a forced win rather than hanging), so direction and exact material are mixed.

1513.label: From a winning (occasionally equal) position, the player throws away the advantage by failing to grab a clear win—most often a hanging/free enemy piece, sometimes by merely threatening a piece instead of capturing it—with a couple of boards instead hanging the player's own material.

1496.label: From a clearly winning middlegame the player throws away the advantage—most often by playing a natural/greedy move that allows a tactical refutation winning back the player's own material (varied piece), and in a minority of boards by overlooking a forced mate with an otherwise safe move.

1516.label: From a (usually winning) middlegame the player most often plays a safe but slower move that skips the cleanest forced win/mate, while a sizable minority instead hang their own queen — so direction is mixed, but the queen is the decisive piece in nearly every board.

1511.chip: Unsound forcing check/sac in king attack
1511.label: In a mostly winning king-attack position, the player abandons the calm winning or saving move for a flashy/forcing try — usually an unsound check or sacrifice (no single piece consistently lost) — that hangs material or lets the attack fizzle, with a few cases being quiet moves that abandon defense or skip a forcing win.

1881.label: In a winning/better position the player makes a lesser capture (often grabbing a pawn) and overlooks a stronger capture of hanging enemy material — an undefended rook or queen, or winning the exchange — throwing away the win; 2-3 boards instead hang the player's own piece (knight/rook) or are non-blunders.

1901.chip: Missed forcing win, played quiet move
1901.label: In winning/decisive endgames the player chooses a quiet material-safe or passive move that skips a faster forcing win (mate, fork, capture, or immediate promotion) — and on two boards a forcing saving capture — though ~3 of the flagged boards were actually optimal.

1902.chip: Trades rook into worse pawn endgame
1902.label: Mostly fires on exchanging a major piece (usually a rook, sometimes the queen) to simplify into a misjudged worse-or-losing pawn endgame, but the set is mixed: ~5/10 fit that core, two boards are non-mistakes (optimal/negligible), one is a tiny inaccuracy, and two hang a piece outright.

1823.label: A middlegame move (97%) that squanders a winning or better position by failing to find the single precise move the position required—and that move is almost always a rook to a critical open file or seventh rank, or a rook-based defensive resource (Rd1/Rd7/Re1/Rc7/Re8 in 7-9 of 10 boards); the punishment is a clean material loss (~6/10, hanging a rook or bishop to a tactic the abandoned move would have prevented, sometimes via fork/discovery) and slow positional/tempo drift the rest, so it is genuinely mixed between hung-own-material and positional drift, with the rook as the one piece in the decisive play of nearly every board.

1895.label: Across mostly endgames the player makes a passive, retreating, or simplifying move that surrenders activity/initiative and worsens the result (throwing a win, a draw, or accelerating a loss); the piece (rook, queen, king, bishop, pawn) and the prior result-state vary, so no single piece or winning/drawn/losing state dominates and the SEE 'rook/drawn/hangs 100%' signature is unreliable.

1922.label: Fires on single-move ~one-piece material swings—predominantly hanging the player's own piece (7/10: bishop, knight, pawn, queen, rook), but also missing a free enemy piece (3/10); a knight is the most common actor though its role and the piece lost both vary too much to pin down.

1865.label: On most boards the player throws away a winning or equal position by playing a flashy check or capture (commonly a bishop/queen sac on f7/f2, sometimes a knight) that hangs own material or walks into mate, though ~3 boards are instead quiet moves that simply miss a clean win.

1923.label: Advances a passed pawn one square toward promotion (e2/d2/b7/c7/f7) instead of first improving piece activity or inserting a preparatory move, letting the opponent plant a clean blockade in front of the pawn and neutralize the advantage.

1906.label: Fires on natural-looking quiet/repositioning moves—most often a bishop—that ignore the position's tactical demands; the plurality hang material or allow a decisive shot (often by removing a defender), but several boards instead miss a forced mate/winning attack or simply lose tempo, so the error type is mixed.

1943.label: A single eval-flipping blunder in which the queen is the decisive piece on ~6-7 of 10 boards, but the role is genuinely mixed — the player hangs their own queen (#1,2,5,9) on some and fails to win/capture the enemy queen or queen-promotion (#3,7,8) on others, with a few non-queen king-safety/positional/missed-win outliers (#4,6,10).

1933.label: Mixed feature: most often hangs the player's own piece by moving away its sole defender or overextending it (rook/knight/bishop victims, queen frequently the abandoning piece), but roughly a third of boards instead skip a winning tactic — so it fires broadly on 'throws away a winning/equal position.'

1928.label: In the opening (mostly), a natural developing or space-gaining move loses the player's own material to a tactic — and a knight is in the decisive play of nearly every board (own knight left hanging on boards 1/6/7, enemy knight fork on 2/4/9, knight ideas on 8) — though two boards (3, 5) are purely positional and two (8, 10) are missed wins rather than material hangs.

1929.label: The player initiates a capture or exchange (9/10 captures, varied piece — knight, rook, queen, bishop) that backfires, either hanging material to the recapture/refutation (≈5 boards) or simplifying into a lost endgame or strategically worse position (≈5 boards); no single piece recurs, so the feature detects 'ill-judged exchanges that lose material or the resulting position' rather than any specific piece blunder.

1949.label: In a (usually) winning endgame the player makes a non-decisive move instead of the material-winning one—about half skip a free winning capture (often grabbing the enemy queen via Rxd4/Rxd3/Rxf5/fxe5) and half instead hang their own piece by removing a key defender or blocker—so the direction and piece are genuinely mixed, plus two boards are already lost where the played move is actually best.

1948.label: In endgames, a king or rook move creates a vulnerable alignment (back-rank, shared rank/file, or stalemate geometry) that lets the opponent's forcing rook check decide the game—winning the rook, forcing a trade into a lost pawn endgame, or delivering mate/stalemate—converting a winning, drawn, or (most often) defensible losing position into a clear loss.

1903.label: In the opening the player makes a tempting material grab (usually a capture, but the piece varies — bishop/queen/knight) instead of the one accurate move and is refuted by an overlooked intermezzo or check, squandering the advantage; ~3 of 10 are non-captures or unsound sacrifices and several start equal/losing, so the 'greedy capture missing the priority move' core is only loosely reliable.

1947.chip: Greedy capture ignores tactic, loses material
1947.label: On most boards the player makes a natural materialistic move—usually a greedy capture or a piece placed on an attacked square—that overlooks the opponent's refutation (often a discovered attack/check) and loses material or the game, but roughly 3-4 boards are instead missed wins or defensive/positional omissions, so the feature is mixed.

1930.label: While winning, the player throws away the advantage by relocating, trading, or otherwise abandoning a dominant/deeply-infiltrated piece (most often a knight, but also queen or bishop) so it gets captured or neutralized in the refutation, instead of consolidating or making the decisive capture.

1957.label: A natural developing/positional move that ignores the position's critical tactical demand—with a knight almost always the decisive piece (hung, forking, or misplaced)—losing material on ~6/10 boards (3 of them to a knight fork) while the rest merely squander a winning or equal position.

1989.label: The played move ignores a pre-existing checkmate from an enemy queen-bishop battery (Qxg2#/Qxg7#/Qxc7#), walking the king into immediate mate when only an interposition saved it; a minority of boards instead simply hang a piece or lose material.

1912.chip: Passive king move skips free capture
1912.label: In a lost endgame the player makes a passive or retreating move (usually a king move) that declines the optimal move — most often a free capture of hung enemy material (rook/queen/knight/pawn) — though a minority of cases are just suboptimal passive king placement with nothing to take.

1942.label: A forcing/aggressive move (capture, check, or intended fork/double-attack played for tempo or material) backfires—most often hanging the player's own piece or exposing the king when the opponent ignores the threat and counterattacks (6–7/10), though two boards are actually missed wins and one isn't a blunder, so neither the piece nor the direction is fully consistent.

1963.label: Mostly fires on position-wrecking blunders—usually a greedy capture or pointless check—that hang the player's own material (rook in #2, queen in #3, bishop in #4/#7, knight in #8, piece varying by board) and turn a defensible or drawn position into a lost one, but a meaningful minority (#1 king walk, #5 pawn-push, #6 spite check) are pure tempo/endgame slips with no material hung, so it's genuinely mixed and a human should review.

1966.chip: Faulty endgame defense, converts to loss
1966.label: In mostly endgames, the player makes a passive/own-agenda move (often a king or pawn advance) that ignores the opponent's one decisive threat—turning a holdable or drawn position into a lost one—but the punishing mechanism varies widely (fork/discovery hanging a rook or bishop, an unstoppable passed pawn, or forced mate), so no single piece or tactic is the invariant.

2008.label: The feature mostly fires on self-inflicted material loss from an over-aggressive capture or check (8/10 are captures, several with check) that gets refuted and drops a piece or—most commonly—the exchange, though the lost material varies (knight, bishop, rook/exchange) and a couple of boards are purely positional (b5c6, h5f3) or lead to mate (e6e5) rather than a clean material drop.

1985.label: In 8 of 10 boards the best move is a winning simplifying capture—typically a queen or rook trade/sacrifice that liquidates a won position into a trivially winning pawn/king endgame (Qxf7+, Qxf6+, Qxe2+, Qxf2+, Rxc7+, Rxf6+)—but the player instead plays a check or a passive/keeping-pieces-on move; a minority of boards (1, 4, and partly 8) instead outright hang the player's own queen, so the feature is mildly mixed but dominated by 'missed winning simplification into endgame'.

2015.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player (almost always with a king move) marches the king the wrong direction or burns a tempo in the pawn race—squandering a win or draw without hanging material—but the feature is impure since roughly four of the top boards are actually 0–7cp non-blunders that merely share the pawn-endgame/king-tempo setting.

1994.label: Fires when the player makes a slow, routine, or loosening move that squanders a winning or equal position by skipping a decisive tactic—most often the knight capture Nxe6 (5/10)—though several boards instead self-inflict material loss by hanging a pawn/piece or grabbing material greedily.

2020.label: Plays an unsound premature queen check to h4/h5 (Qh4+/Qh5+) that is refuted by a simple pawn block (g3/g6) gaining tempo against the queen, squandering the advantage and frequently hanging material — often the queen itself to Nxh5/Nxh4 or a now-undefended knight/pawn.

2018.chip: Trade away key piece, worsening loss
2018.label: In a usually-losing position the player makes a capture or trade—frequently surrendering their own most active/defensive piece—that fails to rescue and often accelerates the loss, though several boards are already dead-lost or are missed captures/failed sacs rather than true trades.

2014.label: In king-and-pawn endgames the player fails to make the decisive king maneuver (infiltration, centralization, or blockade) that wins or holds—most often pushing a pawn instead, or stepping the king the wrong way—squandering the result without ever hanging material.

2021.chip: Exposes own king to decisive check
2021.label: Mostly self-inflicted king-safety blunders: a king move or a tempting capture opens lines/squares so the opponent answers with a decisive check that forces mate or wins material with tempo (boards 1,3,5,6,9,10, plus partials 2,7), but the feature is mixed — two are plain piece-hangs where the king simply can't recapture (4) or a bishop is left en prise (2) and one is a missed win (8).

2005.label: In opening positions—often an f3/e5/g4-bishop gambit-type structure—the player loses material or squanders an advantage, most commonly by hanging or mishandling the light-squared bishop on g4 against a knight on e5, but the specific error varies widely across direct hangs, a fork, a pin, a missed en-passant (exf3), king-safety weakening, and pure positional drops, so this is a mixed feature rather than one clean motif.

2010.label: In a winning or clearly better position the player passes up the forcing tactical continuation (capture, check, promotion, or mating sacrifice), instead playing a greedy capture or a slow/non-forcing move—about half the time this also hangs own material, while the rest simply abandon a forced win or mate.

2039.label: Across the set the player grabs material with a greedy capture (a pawn or bishop) that decisively backfires via the queen—7-8 boards open the d-file or a diagonal and lose their own queen outright (Qxd5/Qxd4/Qxd8/pin), while two are greedy queen-grabs that walk into Bxf7+ Nd5# mate and one merely misses a bigger capture, so the queen is the recurring decisive piece but the punishment isn't uniform.

2040.label: On most boards the player forces a queen trade (via capture/check) that surrenders an available perpetual-check draw and walks into a lost pawn/rook endgame, but the feature is mixed—several boards instead hang the queen, capture the wrong rook, drop the exchange via a pointless check, or contain no real error.

2026.label: From a winning position the player makes a self-inflicting move that throws away the advantage—most often by exposing its own king to a check, discovered attack, or mate—though the feature is mixed and also fires on missed forced mates, a greedy capture, and an endgame slip.

2033.label: In the opening, with an undefended central e-pawn that the knight can grab (Nxe4/Nxe5 is the engine's top move in 9/10 boards), the player instead plays a slow developing pawn or bishop move and skips the free material — though ~4/10 boards also self-hang a piece in the refutation, making the consequence mixed between missed-win and hung-piece.

1990.label: GENUINELY MIXED: the feature fires on opening/early-middlegame central pawn-break moments (the d4/e5/e4 tension and the c3-knight/e3-bishop axis) where the player gets the break decision wrong, but the direction is not consistent — ~4 boards MISS a winning break or free capture (d4 forking c3/e3 in 1, 4, 5; e5 forking f6/d6 in 10; free Bxd6 in 3), ~3-4 boards HANG own material by an unsound advance (bishop in 7, knight after e4 in 8, pawn after f5 in 9), and ~2 are positional collapses after a premature ...e5 (2, 6); the unifying thread is a central pawn-structure/break judgment, not a single piece or single mistake-type, so confidence is low and review is needed.
